desc:
Given two strings s and t, count in how many different ways t can be obtained as a subsequence of s. A subsequence keeps the original order of the characters it keeps; two ways are different if they use a different set of positions in s, even when the resulting letters are the same.

For example, t = "rabbit" can be picked from s = "rabbbit" in 3 ways (any one of the three bs can be left out), and t = "bag" can be picked from s = "babgbag" in 5 ways. If t cannot be formed, return 0.
constraints: s and t consist of lowercase letters and digits
The answer (and every intermediate count in the standard table) fits in a signed 32-bit integer
hints: Enumerating every subsequence of s is exponential. Look at the last character of s and ask how it can be used.

Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways to form the first j characters of t from the first i characters of s. The last character of s is either skipped or, if it equals t[j-1], used as the last character of the match.
ways[i][j] = ways[i-1][j] + (ways[i-1][j-1] if s[i-1] == t[j-1] else 0), with ways[i][0] = 1. The table can be compressed to one row if j is iterated downwards.
editorial: Use dynamic programming over prefixes. Let ways[i][j] be the number of ways the prefix t[:j] is a subsequence of s[:i]. The empty target can be formed in exactly one way (take nothing), so ways[i][0] = 1, and a non-empty target cannot be formed from an empty source, so ways[0][j] = 0 for j > 0. For the general case, either the character s[i-1] is not used, contributing ways[i-1][j], or it is matched with t[j-1] (only possible when they are equal), contributing ways[i-1][j-1].

Each row depends only on the previous one, so a single array of length len(t)+1 suffices as long as the inner loop runs from high j to low j; this avoids using the character s[i-1] twice. Time is O(|s| · |t|), about a million updates for the largest input. Plain recursion without memoisation repeats the same sub-problems and is exponential.
